title: the pillar that's about money
hook: the pillar that's about money; 2.5% and why
carry: what you give purifies what you keep
tomorrow: an orphan, a merchant, a man who was trusted before he was believed

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ramadan, the month of fasting. Your line was hunger teaches. What did the first bite or sip teach you? Day nineteen.

Here's something people don't expect. Of the five pillars that hold up a Muslim life, one is a statement of faith, one is prayer, one is fasting, one is a journey. And one is about your bank balance. Not a suggestion to be nice to the poor sometimes. A number. Worked out once a year, like a tax return, with a calculator and sometimes a spreadsheet. Grandparents do it at the kitchen table with a pencil. Mosques run online calculators for it. It sounds like the least spiritual thing in the whole religion. And its name means something close to purity.
screen: `FIVE PILLARS, ONE ABOUT MONEY.` → `A NUMBER, ONCE A YEAR.` → `ITS NAME MEANS PURITY.`

segments.voice: Zakat. The root, z-k-w, holds two ideas at once: to be pure, and to grow. Think of pruning a plant. You cut some away, and what's left is cleaner, and it grows better. That's the picture. The Qur'an almost never mentions prayer without it. Again and again, in Pickthall's words: “Establish worship, pay the poor-due.” Prayer and zakat, side by side, God and neighbor in one breath. So how does it work? Once a lunar year, a Muslim whose savings stay above a set threshold, called the nisab, traditionally measured in gold or silver, gives two and a half percent of that wealth. One fortieth. Not of income, of what you've held on to for a year. Why so small? Scholars point out that it's meant to be something anyone above the line can give every single year without being ruined by it, and so it never stops. Where does it go? The Qur'an names eight kinds of people: the poor, the needy, those who collect it, people whose hearts are being won over, freeing captives, people crushed by debt, the cause of God, and the stranded traveler. And the money isn't treated as a gift from the giver. It's the poor's right, already inside your wealth, which you're handing back. Many Shia Muslims also give khums, a fifth of their yearly surplus. And beyond all of this is sadaqa, giving from the heart, any amount, anytime. A hadith in Tirmidhi counts even a smile at your brother as sadaqa. Another, in Muslim, says charity never made anyone's wealth smaller.
screen: `ZAKAT — TO PURIFY, TO GROW.` · `PRAYER AND ZAKAT, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `TWO AND A HALF PERCENT, ONCE A YEAR.` · `THE POOR'S RIGHT, HANDED BACK.` · then, large: `ESTABLISH WORSHIP, PAY THE POOR-DUE.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Think about what you have right now. Not only money. Time this week, food in the kitchen, a skill, a coat you haven't worn in two years. Let one thing come to mind that you've been holding on to longer than you need. Picture the pruning: that one thing cut away and handed on. Notice how the rest of what you have feels after it. Lighter, or heavier? Just notice. If you pray, you can offer that thing to God before you give it. The bell holds the time.
Zakat. The third pillar: two and a half percent of savings, given once a year, from a root meaning to purify and to grow. Nineteenth word.
Your line: what you give purifies what you keep. Today, give away one thing, a coin, a coat, an hour, or just a smile, and see what happens to the rest. Day nineteen.

howItsDone: Muslims whose savings are above the nisab threshold calculate zakat once a lunar year, usually 2.5 percent, and give it to people in the categories the Qur'an names, often through a mosque or charity; many time it for Ramadan.

original.note: Arabic: the third pillar, from z-k-w, to be pure and to grow.

trapdoor: what you thought: a religious tax.
what it means: zakat — two and a half percent of savings, given yearly, understood as the poor's right, already inside your wealth.
what a scholar hears: z-k-w joins purity and growth, like pruning; the Qur'an pairs it with prayer again and again; and 9:60 names eight kinds of recipients.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2588 (charity does not decrease wealth)

notes: Pickthall 2:43 quoted from memory ('Establish worship, pay the poor-due, and bow your heads with those who bow (in worship).'). Confirm wording.
Zakat rules simplified: 2.5% on savings/trade goods held a lunar year (hawl) above the nisab (traditionally 85g gold or 595g silver); different rates for crops and livestock not mentioned. Confirm.
Eight categories of 9:60 paraphrased; 'the cause of God' (fi sabil Allah) is interpreted variously. Confirm the list's wording.

'The poor's right, already inside your wealth': drawn from 51:19 and 70:24–25 ('in their wealth is a known right for the beggar and the deprived'); not cited as a quote. A Keeper may want 70:24–25 added to sources.
Khums: obligatory for Twelver Shia on yearly surplus; described as 'many Shia Muslims'. Confirm.
Hadith numbers (Tirmidhi 1956; Muslim 2588) cited from memory; confirm.
The practice ('if you pray, you can offer that thing to God') is an invitation, not a written prayer.
